question: Across six low-dimensional forward PDE instances, do 2022-era vanilla physics-informed neural networks offer a better accuracy-cost tradeoff than piecewise-linear FEniCS finite elements for one-off solution and later pointwise evaluation?

key_findings.claim: The defensible headline is a configuration-specific negative result: the tested vanilla PINNs do not beat the tested FEM stack as one-off forward solvers.
key_findings.evidence: Across 1D/2D/3D Poisson, 1D Allen-Cahn, and 1D/2D semilinear Schrödinger, FEM is generally faster at matched or better discrete relative l2 error; the authors narrow the exception to inconclusive real/imaginary components in 1D Schrödinger and an online evaluation advantage in 3D Poisson.

key_findings.claim: The study is a comparison of one vanilla strong-form PINN recipe against one basic P1 FEniCS recipe, not a comparison of method classes at their frontiers.
key_findings.evidence: PINNs are fully connected tanh networks trained on sampled strong-form PDE, boundary, and initial residuals with Adam followed by L-BFGS; FEM uses FEniCS, piecewise-linear elements, and standard iterative solvers. Adaptive, variational, domain-decomposed, high-order, multigrid, GPU, and operator-learning alternatives are excluded.

key_findings.claim: The stated use of different finite-element bases is contradicted by the experiment descriptions.
key_findings.evidence: The contributions section says the study employs different finite-element bases, but every detailed PDE experiment specifies piecewise-linear P1 elements; there is no p-order, basis-family, or continuity ablation.

key_findings.claim: For 1D Poisson, FEM dominates both the offline and online comparisons.
key_findings.evidence: Across 64 to 4096 P1 cells and fifteen PINN architectures trained on 256 collocation points, PINN training is reported two to three orders of magnitude slower; FEM is also faster and more accurate when interpolation is compared with network evaluation.

key_findings.claim: For 2D Poisson, PINN point evaluation is faster only against an acknowledged inefficient FEM interpolation path.
key_findings.evidence: FEM solve time is one to three orders faster and more accurate. Network evaluation is two to three orders faster than FEniCS interpolation, but the paper notes that FEM solving itself is faster than its interpolation and attributes this inversion to possibly inefficient interpolation code.

key_findings.claim: 3D Poisson is the only convincing reported online-query win, but it does not establish high-dimensional scaling.
key_findings.evidence: Training remains one to three orders slower, while PINN evaluation is two to three orders faster than FEM interpolation at similar or lower relative error. The later claim of no 2D-to-3D cost increase compares only dimensions two and three under different collocation counts, architectures, equations, meshes, and evaluation loads, so it cannot support a curse-of-dimensionality conclusion.

key_findings.claim: Allen-Cahn exposes a sharp-interface and optimization failure regime for vanilla PINNs.
key_findings.evidence: At epsilon 0.01, 20-node-per-layer networks fail, 100- and 500-node networks improve, and FEM is five to six orders faster in reported solution time and about one order faster in evaluation. At epsilon 0.001, all tried PINN architectures and activations fail while FEM produces a solution; the authors point to strong-form conditioning and suggest adaptive or variational PINNs.

key_findings.claim: For 1D Schrödinger, FEM wins on the physically aggregated modulus even though component-wise comparisons are inconclusive.
key_findings.evidence: For the modulus, FEM is about two orders faster in solution time and more accurate, and FEM interpolation is also faster and more accurate than PINN evaluation. PINN evaluation is about one order faster only when compared with a fresh FEM solve; real and imaginary component accuracy results are mixed.

key_findings.claim: For 2D Schrödinger, PINNs miss fine wave structure and remain slower than FEM in both reported phases.
key_findings.evidence: The PINN approximations lose features near the right boundary while finer FEM meshes recover them. FEM is reported two to three orders faster for solving and about one order faster for evaluation; the PINN imaginary component is substantially less accurate, although its evaluation can slightly beat a fresh FEM solve at similar aggregate error.

key_findings.claim: The evaluation protocol is not a hardware-normalized, accuracy-matched solver benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: FEM runs on CPU while PINNs train and evaluate on a Quadro P6000 GPU; fixed epoch budgets and manually chosen learning rates, loss weights, and architectures exclude tuning cost. Only discrete relative l2 error and wall time are reported, without memory, energy, FLOPs, matched stopping, compilation, warm-up, or confidence intervals.

key_findings.claim: Time-dependent accuracy is measured against an uncertified FEM-derived reference rather than an independent truth.
key_findings.evidence: Poisson uses analytic solutions, but Allen-Cahn and both Schrödinger tasks use fine-mesh implicit-Euler FEM as ground truth. The paper invokes general convergence theory but provides no grid/time-step refinement certificate or bound for the particular reference, and candidate FEM shares its discretization family.

key_findings.claim: The official artifact contradicts the claimed epochwise Latin-hypercube resampling.
key_findings.evidence: At current official-repository HEAD f295ec6, each Adam training_step is JIT-compiled yet calls host-side pyDOE.lhs inside the compiled function and returns its PRNG key unchanged. Those NumPy samples are materialized during tracing and reused, rather than newly generated each epoch as pages 6, 7, 8, and 15 state.

key_findings.claim: The released Schrödinger PINNs do not implement the stated space-time problems.
key_findings.evidence: Both released Schrödinger scripts sample residual points only for t in [0,1], while the paper specifies and evaluates t in [0,pi/2], leaving about 36 percent of the target interval as unconstrained extrapolation. The 1D script also enforces periodic values but omits the periodic spatial-derivative term explicitly present in the paper's loss.

anchors.section: 1D Schrödinger PINN loss and collocation domain
2D Schrödinger PINN loss and collocation domain

key_findings.claim: The released 2D Schrödinger PINN path is statically non-runnable as written.
key_findings.evidence: Schroedinger_2D/util.py returns two-column initial points [x,y], but 2D_Semilinear_Schrödinger.py:init_residual accesses points[:,2]. The first compiled loss evaluation should therefore index a nonexistent third column, so the current checkout cannot reproduce Figure 13 without correction or unreleased code.

key_findings.claim: Two released FEM scripts underreport average solution time by a factor of ten if they generated the plotted data.
key_findings.evidence: FEM codes/1D_Allen-Cahn.py and FEM codes/2D_Schroedinger.py reset time_solving inside each of ten repetitions and then divide only the final repetition by ten. This does not erase the qualitative Allen-Cahn gap, but it invalidates exact ratios and shifts the affected FEM points by one order of magnitude; time-dependent solve timing also includes per-step HDF5 output.

key_findings.claim: The official repository is a useful implementation sketch but not an archival reproduction package for the arXiv revision.
key_findings.evidence: The current checkout has no license, tests, CI, environment lock, result tables, or plotting scripts; key 1D/2D Schrödinger and 3D Poisson evaluation files are absent, including an unanswered issue requesting the promised 1D Schrödinger truth. Commits in 2024 also changed Allen-Cahn nonlinearity and Schrödinger time stepping after arXiv v1.

method.core_idea: Put vanilla PINN and finite-element approximations on time-versus-relative-error plots for the same six PDE instances, separating the cost of obtaining a solution from the cost of evaluating that solution on a new point set.
method.mechanism: For PINNs, minimize sampled strong-form PDE plus boundary/initial residuals with fully connected tanh networks, Adam, and L-BFGS; for FEM, discretize weak forms with P1 elements in FEniCS and standard linear or Newton solvers. Evaluate both against analytic Poisson truth or fine-FEM time-dependent references and average nominally ten wall-clock runs.
assumptions: A single-instance, low-dimensional forward solve is the intended workload.
Discrete relative l2 error on one evaluation mesh captures solution quality.
Fine-mesh implicit-Euler FEM is an accurate enough reference for Allen-Cahn and Schrödinger without an instance-specific error certificate.
CPU FEniCS timing and GPU JAX timing are meaningfully comparable as method costs.
P1 FEniCS with the selected solver and interpolation path represents the relevant FEM baseline.
Heuristically selected architectures, weights, and fixed epoch budgets represent vanilla PINN performance without charging tuning cost.
The public code implements the paper protocol and the ten nominal repeats represent stochastic variation.
Two-to-three-dimensional Poisson behavior is informative about genuinely high-dimensional scaling.

techniques.role: Encodes the differential equation and conditions as sampled mean-square residuals.
Computes PDE derivatives through JAX automatic differentiation.
Selects collocation, boundary, and initial points across each domain.
Uses first-order training followed by quasi-Newton refinement.
Weights and pretrains the Allen-Cahn initial condition after direct full-loss training proves difficult.
Uses piecewise-linear finite elements as the sole classical discretization family.
Provides mesh, weak-form assembly, solvers, interpolation, and time stepping.
Separates offline solution/training cost from online interpolation/network-query cost.
Measures both methods on a common discrete evaluation set.
Repeats Poisson in one, two, and three dimensions to probe cost changes.

evaluations.setting: 1D Poisson on [0,1], analytic truth; 64-4096 P1 cells versus fifteen tanh PINNs with 256 collocation points.
evaluations.metric: Wall-clock solve/train and interpolate/evaluate time versus discrete relative l2 error.
evaluations.result: FEM is faster and more accurate in both phases; PINN training is two to three orders slower.
evaluations.baseline: FEniCS P1 conjugate-gradient solve with incomplete-LU preconditioning.

evaluations.setting: 2D mixed-boundary Poisson, analytic truth; 100^2-1000^2 P1 meshes versus eleven PINN architectures with 2000 domain and 250 boundary samples.
evaluations.metric: Solution and new-grid evaluation time versus discrete relative l2 error.
evaluations.result: FEM solves one to three orders faster and more accurately; PINN query is two to three orders faster than an acknowledged inefficient FEM interpolation path but remains less accurate.
evaluations.baseline: Triangular P1 FEniCS with conjugate gradient and incomplete-LU preconditioning.

evaluations.setting: 3D Dirichlet Poisson on the unit cube, analytic truth; 16^3-128^3 cube meshes split into tetrahedra versus eight PINNs with 1000 domain and 100 boundary samples.
evaluations.metric: Train/solve and evaluation/interpolation time versus relative l2 error on a 150^3 grid.
evaluations.result: PINN training is one to three orders slower, but selected PINNs reach similar or better error; PINN query is two to three orders faster than FEM interpolation and is the paper's sole clear online win.
evaluations.baseline: Tetrahedral P1 FEniCS with conjugate gradient and incomplete-LU preconditioning.

evaluations.setting: 1D Allen-Cahn to T=0.05 at epsilon 0.01 and stress test at epsilon 0.001; four P1 meshes versus fourteen weighted/pretrained PINNs.
evaluations.metric: Solve/evaluation time, relative l2 error, visual interface recovery, and training success.
evaluations.result: At epsilon 0.01 FEM is reported five to six orders faster to solve and about one order faster to evaluate; at epsilon 0.001 vanilla PINNs fail across attempted activations while FEM succeeds.
evaluations.baseline: Periodic P1 FEniCS time stepping with Newton solves and a fine implicit-Euler FEM reference.

evaluations.setting: 1D focusing semilinear Schrödinger on [-5,5] through pi/2; four P1 meshes versus eight complex-output PINNs.
evaluations.metric: Time versus relative l2 error for real part, imaginary part, and modulus.
evaluations.result: On modulus, FEM solves about two orders faster and is more accurate; FEM evaluation also wins, while component-wise accuracy is inconclusive. Released PINN code trains residuals only through t=1 and omits derivative periodicity.
evaluations.baseline: Periodic P1 FEniCS semi-implicit stepping with GMRES and fine-FEM reference.

evaluations.setting: 2D semilinear Schrödinger on [-5,5]^2 through pi/2; five P1 meshes versus six complex-output PINNs with 5000 domain samples.
evaluations.metric: Visual feature recovery and time versus relative l2 error for real, imaginary, and modulus components.
evaluations.result: FEM is reported two to three orders faster to solve and one order faster to evaluate; PINNs miss fine boundary features and have poor imaginary-part accuracy. The released PINN path has an invalid initial-point index and the FEM timer underreports by tenfold.
evaluations.baseline: Periodic triangular P1 FEniCS with semi-implicit GMRES stepping and fine-FEM reference.

evaluations.setting: Official artifact at current HEAD f295ec6bb4b746e0029bff5b5f512fb949603256, inspected on 2026-08-23.
evaluations.metric: Static compilation, protocol-to-code trace, dependency/release completeness, committed evaluation assets, and commit history.
evaluations.result: Python compileall succeeds, but epochwise sampling, Schrödinger domains/conditions, 2D initialization, and two FEM timers contradict the paper; evaluation assets and reproducibility infrastructure are incomplete, and post-paper commits alter protocols.
evaluations.baseline: The methods, ten-repeat averaging, and public-code availability claimed on pages 6-8, 15, 18, and 21.

limitations: Author-stated: the experiments cover vanilla PINNs, not adaptive, variational, domain-decomposed, or other specialized variants.
Author-stated: only the 3D Poisson experiment shows a clear network point-evaluation advantage, and repeatedly solving FEM may still be cheaper than training once.
Author-stated: parameterized PDE/operator-learning amortization is not studied.

Only six single-instance, smooth or phase-field, one-to-three-dimensional forward problems are tested; inverse, data-assisted, noisy, geometric, parameter-family, and truly high-dimensional regimes are absent.
Every reported FEM experiment uses P1 elements despite the stated contribution of multiple bases; no adaptive, hp, high-order, spectral, multigrid, matrix-free, or GPU FEM appears.
CPU FEM and GPU PINN wall times are not hardware-, throughput-, energy-, or cost-normalized.
Architecture, learning-rate, loss-weight, and pretraining choices are manual and PDE-specific, but their search cost is excluded.
Fixed training epochs are not matched-accuracy or matched-budget stopping rules.
The only numerical accuracy metric is discrete relative l2; no H1, maximum error, conservation, stability, or continuous residual certificate is reported.
Fine-FEM time-dependent references are not independently certified by a reported refinement study or bound.
Ten timing runs have no confidence intervals, failure probabilities, or accuracy variation, and released PINN initialization is reset to the same seed each run.
FEM point evaluation uses an acknowledged inefficient Python interpolation path, making online conclusions implementation-bound.
Official code lacks a locked environment, tests, CI, license, release DOI, result tables, and plotting pipeline, and several required evaluation arrays are absent.
Current artifact code differs from arXiv v1 after 2024 Allen-Cahn and Schrödinger edits.
Multiple artifact defects require corrected reruns before exact Schrödinger and Allen-Cahn/2D-Schrödinger timing ratios can be trusted.
failure_modes: A strong-form residual becomes ill-conditioned around sharp interfaces or multiscale features, so an expressive network never reaches the desired solution.
Loss components converge at different rates; manual weighting or initial-condition pretraining makes the result protocol-dependent.
Finite collocation and evaluation grids miss localized residual violations, spurious solutions, or conservation failures.
Host-side random sampling inside a JIT trace silently becomes fixed collocation, invalidating an intended resampling experiment.
Training on a truncated time interval turns late-time evaluation into extrapolation while appearing to solve the full stated PDE.
Omitting derivative periodicity underconstrains a periodic Schrödinger problem even when periodic values match.
A shape/index error in initial-condition construction prevents a released experiment from running.
Resetting a timer inside the repeat loop and dividing once more reports one tenth of the actual mean.
Including disk output inside solve time conflates numerical work with storage performance.
A slow general interpolation API creates a misleading online advantage over an optimized classical evaluator.
A fine instance of the same FEM family used as truth hides common discretization bias and can rank candidate FEM unfairly.
A two-to-three-dimensional comparison with changed workloads is extrapolated to a high-dimensional scaling claim.
Offline training never amortizes because the workload contains too few repeated point queries or related PDE instances.
A negative result for one 2022 recipe is generalized to modern PINNs, neural operators, or hybrid solvers.
reusable_insights: Separate one-off construction cost, point-query cost, and family-level amortized cost; report the break-even query count.
Benchmark at equal error and equal cost with optimized, independently reviewed baselines on matched hardware.
Charge hyperparameter search, reference generation, compilation, warm-up, memory, and energy to the appropriate phase.
Use independent references or certify reference discretization error with refinement and a posteriori bounds.
Report multiple norms, continuous-domain residual certificates, conservation/stability checks, multiple seeds, failure rates, and confidence intervals.
Trace random-number generation through JIT/graph compilation; an apparent sampling call can be constant after tracing.
Machine-check the sampled training domain and every boundary/initial term against the mathematical problem statement.
Keep timing accumulation outside repeat loops and isolate I/O from solver timing with tests for known synthetic durations.
Treat PINNs and FEM as design spaces rather than singular baselines; include strong modern variants and hybrids.
Negative benchmarks are especially valuable when configurations, artifacts, and counterexamples are reproducible and narrowly claimed.
open_questions: Do the six accuracy-cost frontiers persist after correcting the artifact's sampling, time-domain, boundary, indexing, and timing defects?
How do vanilla and modern PINNs compare with adaptive hp-FEM, multigrid, high-order, matrix-free, and GPU implementations under matched hardware and error?
What online break-even point remains after replacing FEniCS Python interpolation with a preassembled or vectorized evaluator?
Can continuous residual certification predict when discrete relative l2 evaluation has missed a catastrophic PINN failure?
Which combination of causal training, adaptive sampling, domain decomposition, weak residuals, and second-order optimization closes the Allen-Cahn and Schrödinger gaps?
How should one allocate and report architecture, loss-weight, and optimizer tuning budgets fairly across solver families?
What scaling curve appears from dimensions three through genuinely high dimension with the PDE, architecture, sample density, accuracy, and hardware controlled?
When does a PINN or neural operator repay offline training across parameter changes, geometries, initial conditions, or repeated queries?
Can a hybrid FEM-neural method retain classical stability and error control while accelerating repeated solves or fine-scale correction?
How sensitive are the results to random seeds, collocation refresh schedules, and rare training failures once true independent repeats are used?
Would independent spectral, analytic, or rigorously refined references change rankings for the time-dependent equations?
What artifact tests can automatically verify that released code implements every equation, domain, condition, sample schedule, and timer in a paper?

competitive_landscape.title: Physics Informed Deep Learning (Part I): Data-driven Solutions of Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Raissi et al. establish the residual-trained single-instance method and Schrödinger setup used here; the focal paper audits its cost against FEM rather than proposing a solver.

competitive_landscape.title: The Deep Ritz method: A deep learning-based numerical algorithm for solving variational problems
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep Ritz minimizes an energy functional and changes derivative order and optimization geometry; its behavior is not represented by the focal strong-form PINNs.

competitive_landscape.title: DGM: A deep learning algorithm for solving partial differential equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep Galerkin is another mesh-free residual learner with its own architecture and sampling strategy; the focal experiment restricts itself to fully connected vanilla PINNs.

competitive_landscape.title: Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks For Solving Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: VPINNs use Petrov-Galerkin weak residuals and integration by parts, a directly relevant alternative for the focal sharp-interface failures but not benchmarked.

competitive_landscape.title: hp-VPINNs: Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks With Domain Decomposition
competitive_landscape.difference: hp-VPINNs combine local weak forms with hp-style decomposition, testing the hybrid design space that a binary vanilla-PINN-versus-P1-FEM comparison omits.

competitive_landscape.title: The Old and the New: Can Physics-Informed Deep-Learning Replace Traditional Linear Solvers?
competitive_landscape.difference: Markidis directly compares a PINN Poisson solver with conjugate-gradient and multigrid methods before the focal paper, conflicting with any claim that neural and classical solvers had only been studied in isolation.

competitive_landscape.title: A mixed formulation for physics-informed neural networks as a potential solver for engineering problems in heterogeneous domains: comparison with finite element method
competitive_landscape.difference: Rezaei et al. compare mixed PINNs directly with FEM for heterogeneous elasticity and Poisson problems before the focal submission, narrowing the focal novelty to a broader negative multi-PDE timing study.

competitive_landscape.title: PDEBENCH: An Extensive Benchmark for Scientific Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: PDEBench standardizes larger parameterized time-dependent datasets, classical generation, PINN and operator baselines, and richer metrics; its operator-learning workload differs from focal single-instance solves.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding and mitigating gradient pathologies in physics-informed neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. diagnose stiff, imbalanced composite-loss gradients and improve them with adaptive annealing, explaining why focal heuristic weighting and pretraining are not incidental details.

competitive_landscape.title: When and why PINNs fail to train: A neural tangent kernel perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: The NTK analysis attributes unequal convergence of boundary, initial, and PDE terms to spectral imbalance and proposes principled reweighting absent from the focal baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: Characterizing possible failure modes in physics-informed neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Krishnapriyan et al. show that modest PDE coefficient changes can make training ill-conditioned and that curricula help, cautioning against reading focal failures as representational impossibility.

competitive_landscape.title: How to Avoid Trivial Solutions in Physics-Informed Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Leiteritz and Pflüger show that finite collocation can admit trivial low-penalty solutions and study sampling remedies, directly relevant to the focal fixed-after-JIT sample defect.

competitive_landscape.title: Respecting causality is all you need for training physics-informed neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Causal weighting addresses all-at-once time training failures in multiscale dynamics; the focal Allen-Cahn and Schrödinger baselines do not use it.

competitive_landscape.title: A comprehensive study of non-adaptive and residual-based adaptive sampling for physics-informed neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This large empirical sampling study demonstrates that collocation policy materially changes performance; the focal paper claims resampling but its released JIT code instead freezes Adam samples.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Error Certification for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Eiras et al. formally bound continuous residuals for equations including Schrödinger and Allen-Cahn, filling the focal gap left by finite-grid relative l2 evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: An Expert's Guide to Training Physics-informed Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: The guide supplies reproducible JAX ablations and modern training recipes; it is a stronger current PINN baseline than the focal 2022 vanilla stack.

competitive_landscape.title: Challenges in Training PINNs: A Loss Landscape Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: Rathore et al. trace ill-conditioning to differential operators, support Adam-to-L-BFGS for the focal era, and introduce a stronger Nyström Newton-CG alternative.

competitive_landscape.title: Weak baselines and reporting biases lead to overoptimism in machine learning for fluid-related partial differential equations
competitive_landscape.difference: McGreivy and Hakim show weak classical baselines dominate published ML-PDE speedup claims and codify the equal-error, optimized-baseline standard needed to interpret focal results.

competitive_landscape.title: PINNacle: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: PINNacle evaluates about ten PINN methods on more than twenty PDEs with standardized tooling, making the focal six-problem vanilla comparison a historical baseline rather than a current method survey.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics Informed Neural Networks with strong and weak residuals for advection-dominated diffusion problems
competitive_landscape.difference: Sikora et al. compare strong and weak PINN residuals with higher-order stabilized FEM in advection-dominated regimes, expanding both neural and classical baselines beyond focal P1/vanilla choices.

competitive_landscape.title: PirateNets: Physics-informed Deep Learning with Residual Adaptive Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: PirateNets combine adaptive residual architectures with current training practices and target deep-PINN failures, providing a materially stronger Allen-Cahn-style neural baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: Fast training of accurate physics-informed neural networks without gradient descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Frozen-PINN uses random frozen features, space-time separation, and linear solves instead of gradient training, reporting strong efficiency on eight PDE benchmarks; it attacks the focal offline bottleneck directly.

competitive_landscape.title: From Mesh to Neural Nets: A Multi-Method Evaluation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Galerkin Finite Element Method for Solving Nonlinear Convection-Reaction-Diffusion Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Hasan et al. report PINN advantages over GFEM on selected 1D convection-reaction-diffusion equations, a conflicting result whose fairness and efficiency definitions must be reconciled with focal timing discipline.

competitive_landscape.title: DNN-MG: A Hybrid Neural Network/Finite Element Method with Applications to 3D Simulations of the Navier-Stokes Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: DNN-MG learns local fine-scale corrections around a coarse FEM solve and reports large 3D speedups, replacing the focal either-or framing with a practical hybrid.

competitive_landscape.title: Domain decomposition-based coupling of physics-informed neural networks via the Schwarz alternating method
competitive_landscape.difference: Schwarz coupling between PINNs and FE/FD/FV full-order models improves difficult high-Peclet training, supporting complementarity rather than replacement.

competitive_landscape.title: Benchmarking Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Boundary Elements Methods for Wave Scattering
competitive_landscape.difference: The BEM study independently recovers the focal pattern in 2D Helmholtz scattering: classical assembly/solve is roughly four orders faster, while trained PINN point queries are roughly two orders faster.

competitive_landscape.title: Critical evaluation of PINN for FWD inverse analysis and differentiable FEM as an alternative
competitive_landscape.difference: Choi et al. find standard/extended PINNs sensitive and less robust than differentiable FEM on layered pavement inversion, extending the negative comparison into a noisy inverse setting absent from focal.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepONet: Learning nonlinear operators for identifying differential equations based on the universal approximation theorem of operators
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepONet learns function-to-function maps over problem families; its expensive offline phase and fast reuse require a break-even analysis unlike focal one-instance PINN training.

competitive_landscape.title: Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: FNO targets parametric solution operators and very fast repeated inference; a fair classical comparison must include simulation-data generation, training, and query-count amortization.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning the solution operator of parametric partial differential equations with physics-informed DeepOnets
competitive_landscape.difference: Physics-informed DeepONet trains across parameterized PDE families with little or no paired outputs, directly instantiating the many-query regime the focal paper leaves to future work.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Learning Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: PINO combines coarse solution data with fine-resolution physics constraints and operator amortization, a distinct cost model that cannot be rejected by focal single-instance vanilla results.

competitive_landscape.title: The Ill-Posed Foundations of Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Their Finite-Difference Variants
competitive_landscape.difference: Langer shows nonuniqueness and ill-posed objectives can persist for AD and finite-difference PINNs, strengthening the warning that finite sampled residual or l2 values do not certify solver reliability.

competitive_landscape.title: A robust and stable hybrid neural network/finite element method for 2D flows that generalizes to different geometries
competitive_landscape.difference: This DNN-MG successor tests rollout stability, replay-buffer retraining, unstructured meshes, and geometry transfer, showing the current hybrid engineering frontier omitted by focal.

competitive_landscape.title: Derivative Computation in PINNs: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond
competitive_landscape.difference: Mikulski and Uhl show calibrated finite differences can match automatic-differentiation accuracy while reducing time and memory on tested PDEs, challenging focal claims that autodiff is an unqualified computational advantage.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: PINNs and FEM had mainly been studied in isolation, and this paper offers a systematic comparison over elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic equations in one to three dimensions using solution time, evaluation time, and accuracy.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The arXiv revision provides six shared-instance accuracy-cost plots and distinguishes offline solve/train from online interpolation/evaluation, but all FEM experiments use P1 and all neural experiments use one vanilla recipe family.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The broad first-comparison implication is not credible because Markidis 2021 and Rezaei 2022 already perform direct neural/classical or PINN/FEM comparisons, and PDEBench contemporaneously provides a broader SciML benchmark. The defensible novelty is one of the first transparent multi-PDE negative cost-accuracy audits of 2022-era vanilla single-instance PINNs against a consistent P1 FEniCS stack, with offline and online phases separated. Its qualitative one-off-solver conclusion is useful but restricted, and exact Schrödinger and affected timing claims require corrected reruns because the official artifact does not implement the stated protocol. No explicit bit-for-bit independent reproduction of this focal study was found through 2026-08-23; later BEM and differentiable-FEM studies are conceptual replications.

reviewer_notes: Source-locked audit of arXiv v1: all 27 pages, 13 figures, equations, references, and every experimental subsection were read; the paper has no tables or appendix. All pages were rendered and visually inspected, with high-resolution checks of result figures. Three primary-source search families were covered through 2026-08-23: direct PINN/classical benchmarks and replications; PINN failure, sampling, optimization, and certification work; and variational, domain-decomposed, hybrid, and operator-learning alternatives. Official artifact https://github.com/TamaraGrossmann/FEM-vs-PINNs was cloned at current HEAD f295ec6bb4b746e0029bff5b5f512fb949603256 (2024-03-15); python3 -m compileall passes, but no license/tests/CI/lockfile or archival result pipeline exists. Exact static defects: jitted training_step calls host pyDOE.lhs and returns an unchanged key; 1D_Semilinear_Schrödinger.py lines 59-69 omits derivative periodicity and samples t<=1; 2D_Semilinear_Schrödinger.py lines 70-72 indexes column 2 of two-column initial samples and lines 99-101 samples t<=1; FEM codes/1D_Allen-Cahn.py lines 55-84 and FEM codes/2D_Schroedinger.py lines 68-105 divide only the final repetition by ten. Committed Eval_Points lacks the promised 1D Schrödinger solution, all 2D Schrödinger evaluation data, and 3D Poisson evaluation points; issue 1 requesting the missing 1D truth remained open. The 2024 peer-reviewed IMA Journal version (DOI 10.1093/imamat/hxae011) revises some details, so it was not silently mixed into this source-pinned arXiv reading.
